record.tranche_reason: The paper fits scaling laws on synthetic PCFG data and reports that their fitted parameters and compute-optimal frontiers vary with data compressibility, refining the claim that scaling laws are data-agnostic.
record.gate_note: The reported scaling-law fits use final training losses, not held-out losses. The paper does not validate predictions from small runs against runs orders of magnitude larger. Figure 8 reports compressibility measurements, not language-model scaling results.
record.test_reason: The study fits the Hoffmann loss form separately on six synthetic PCFG datasets, about 4M–1.4B parameters and 100K–100M tokens. It reports that the fitted parameters and the compute-optimal split shift with data compressibility. This bears directly on V7's data-dependence and argues that V3's equal (Chinchilla) split is data-specific rather than general.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that Chinchilla-type laws are web-text-specific cases of data-dependent laws. Harder-to-compress data needs more compute and a more data-preferent split. They propose a compressibility-parameterised law and a Chinchilla-adjusted form (Eq. 6). They acknowledge the results are small-scale, synthetic PCFG only, and not yet shown on real data. The StarCoder savings estimate (24% fewer FLOPs) is unvalidated napkin math.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains small transformer LMs on synthetic PCFG token sequences and fits the Hoffmann-style loss form across model and dataset sizes. It analyzes training-loss fits by data compressibility rather than reproducing the original large-scale held-out-loss experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Fitted parameters and the compute-optimal parameter-data preference vary with dataset gzip-compressibility. With terminal count fixed, parameter shifts still track compressibility; when compressibility is roughly fixed, varying syntactic properties does not meaningfully shift the fitted parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Harder-to-compress PCFG data takes longer to converge for all model sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-convergence speed depends on data compressibility.

fits_no_version.finding: In preliminary runs on code datasets (HTML, C, Python), slightly more compute is needed as compressibility rises. No law is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute needed for a target loss rises with data compressibility in code.

record.problems: The scaling-law experiments are restricted to synthetic PCFG data and are described by the authors as small scale. They fit final training losses rather than held-out losses, and do not validate small-run extrapolations. Real-world code results are preliminary and do not include fitted scaling laws. Some results are presented in figures without numeric values; Table 2 reports fitted parameters without uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2's individual model-by-dataset curves and Figure 9's individual code-dataset curves were not extracted as separate rows: the text reports their aggregate trends, while the plotted curves do not provide tabulated numeric values.

untested.parts: Whether loss follows a power law is not assessed. The form is assumed and fitted with no fit-quality reported. Ranges span about 2.5 orders in N and 3 in D.
No extrapolation from small to larger runs is evaluated. The planned 1.92e19-FLOP comparison is not reported.
There is no empirical IsoFLOP search for optimal N and D, and no stability check of the exponents across budgets. Frontiers come only from fitted laws.
Shape is co-varied with size (Tab. 6); there is no fixed-size shape comparison.
No other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer setting is tested. Code results are compressibility measurements and preliminary curves without fitted laws.
Parameter counting, schedule, fitting method and departures from a single power law are not varied. Only data complexity is varied.

missing.what: Linear regressions of each scaling parameter on compressibility H. Slopes: A -16.20 (p=.048), B -24.77 (p=.009), α -0.87 (p=.043), β -2.34 (p=.008); E +3.92 (p=.272, not significant). α and β intersect at H≈0.27.
Parameter-data scaling contours showing that the frontier at compressibility 0.60 needs more compute and prefers data.

record.verdict_notes: I dropped the reader's V3 'supports' label. Per-dataset frontiers are powers of compute by construction, so they cannot support stability. I also dropped the V7 'limits_scope' label from R8: it is a confounder control showing dependence runs through compressibility, not a failure of data-dependence. Several fits have negative E (one is -1693) and α, β above 1, so the fits are poorly constrained, with no uncertainties reported. Training is single-epoch, so final training loss is close to held-out loss, but the paper does not report held-out loss. The study is a single-author preprint.

versions.untested_parts: The reported fits concern final training losses; held-out pretraining loss is not reported.
No small-run fits are evaluated against larger-run losses as an extrapolation test.

The paper derives and plots compute-optimal frontiers for PCFG datasets, but does not report a separate numerical validation of the power exponents governing optimal parameter and token counts across compute budgets.
Architectures vary with parameter count; the paper does not compare architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Real-world code and natural-language scaling laws are not fitted or validated; no other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer setting is tested.

The paper tests variation with training-data complexity and syntactic properties. It does not test parameter-counting choices, training schedules, fitting methods, or departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: PCFG-trained LMs (fitted scaling-law frontiers)
rows.operation_detail: Derive and plot compute-optimal parameter-data frontiers from the fitted scaling laws

conditions.value: 0.12, 0.23, 0.45, and 0.60 in Figure 3; the paper also reports a fit at 0.32

rows.baseline: Chinchilla frontier with a 1-to-1 parameter-data scaling
rows.value: The fitted frontier becomes increasingly data-preferent as data becomes harder to compress; the crossover with Chinchilla is reported at 0.23 < gzip-compressibility < 0.45.
rows.note: The figure plots individual training runs colored by loss; the text states the direction of the frontier shift.
rows.check: For V3, each per-dataset frontier is a power of compute by construction (Eq. 2), so this cannot test stability. What it shows is that the allocation exponent varies with data: parameter-preferent at low compressibility, data-preferent at high, crossing Chinchilla's 1:1 between 0.23 and 0.45. For V7 the state is observed. The Fig. 3 description is qualitative only.

relationships.reason: The equal-split frontier holds only near intermediate compressibility. Easier data is more parameter-preferent than Chinchilla and harder data far more data-preferent (R6, from Tab. 2 exponents).
relationships.display_finding: Across compressibility 0.12–0.60, easier data favored parameters and harder data favored data, with nearly equal allocation only at intermediate compressibility.
